meaning_fix: not (verb negation framing the verb with ma- and -sh, e.g. ma biddish 'I don't want', ma 3irfish 'I didn't know')
reasoning: This is the ma...sh circumfix negation, which is in use in Palestinian speech. It is an ordinary verb negation and not necessarily emphatic. The ellipsis is not romanized, so the two parts are written as 'ma sh'.

A verb built from English 'block' on the fa33al pattern, so the l is doubled: ballak. He-form past, e.g. ballakni 'he blocked me'. I am not fully sure about the shadda, and a phrase like 'amal blook is also possible.
An MSA-origin word that Palestinians say in conversation, as in talawwut il-hawa. Urban speech turns ث into t, so it is respelled with ت. Shadda on و.
ث becomes t in Palestinian, so it is taanye, as in 'tanye wa7de'. Taa marbuta after ي is e.
Urban Levantine 'when', with a long ee. Alif maqsura is written a. Some speakers say imta, so I am only moderately sure of the vowel.

romanization: illi byijri wara id-dunya ma byil7a'ha
vowelled_arabic: اللِّي بْيِجْرِي وَرَا الدُّنْيَا مَا بْيِلْحَقْهَا
reasoning: A colloquial proverb with the bi- present tense and ma for negating the verb. The ق in byil7a'ha is a glottal stop. il- assimilates to د in id-dunya. The byi- vs bi- form of the 3ms verbs is uncertain.
Urban Palestinian turns aw into oo, giving moosim, as in moosim iz-zeetuun for the olive season. It also means a season of fruit or events in general.
An MSA-origin word that is used in conversation. In such words urban speech usually turns ذ into z, giving jazzaab, though jaddaab is also possible. English 'attractive, charming' is accurate.
Uses bi- present tense, 2ms bta3rif, and ween for 'where'. The trailing ellipsis and question mark are not romanized, and il- is kept as an open frame.
il- assimilates to the sun letter ص. Colloquially the final hamza of صحراء is dropped, giving Sa7ra. gharbiyye ends in e after ي.

meaning_fix: fizzy drink / soda (short for mashruub ghaazi; the common everyday noun is feminine, ghaaziyye)
reasoning: ghaazi is the adjective 'carbonated' as a shortened noun. I know it as the fuller mashruub ghaazi, and feminine ghaaziyye (غازية) for a bottle of soda. I am not sure how natural the bare masculine form is.
Construct state of 'wife of the paternal uncle': mart 3amm, with the taa marbuta pronounced t, as in mart 3ammi. 3amm is the father's brother.
A shopping phrase. kiilo is a loan with a long ii, ending in o.

meaning_fix: sit-in / protest in which people gather or stay in one place (a general protest march is muDaahara)
reasoning: An MSA-origin word that is commonly used in Palestinian news and speech. It means a sit-in or an occupation-style protest, not any protest.
Everyday phrase for 'it's on me'. The first vowel of 7isaab drops before the suffix, giving 7saabi.
An English loan ('follow'), used as a noun or verb in social-media talk. The vowel length follows the Arabic spelling, so the exact pronunciation is uncertain.
The short form of nine used before a counted noun, as in tis3 iyyaam. Standing alone it is tis3a.
From qalam 'pen', so lined or striped. ق is a glottal stop and the l is doubled. mkhaTTaT is also used for striped.
ط is emphatic, so a capital T. For a person it means down-to-earth, modest or unpretentious as well as simple, which fits 'easygoing'.
3amme is the paternal aunt, with a doubled m and taa marbuta as e. Said with a suffix it is ibn 3ammti.
A common idiom used in Palestinian speech. ق is a glottal stop in 7ara'. The glottal is written after il- in il-'akhDar, and it is wil-yaabis with the ي as a consonant.
The participle of Tallaq 'divorce', with doubled l, emphatic T and glottal stop for ق. It is not muTlaq 'absolute'.
ق is a glottal stop. The -i ending makes the colour adjective, from burtu'aal 'orange (fruit)'.
A he-form past verb, naja7, with ح as 7. It is used for passing exams, e.g. naja7 bil-imti7aan. najja7 with a doubled j is the causative.
Everyday phrase about the shekel and the dollar. The article assimilates to the sun letter ص, giving iS-Sarf, and si3r is in construct.
